help.intro: A short text of about 150 words about Münster, the German city with more bicycles than people: about 320,000 inhabitants and about half a million bikes. The text tells you where the people of Münster ride (to work, to the university, to the market), what the Radstation at the station is, where a bike can park for 3,300 bikes, and what a Leeze is. The facts are real and were checked. You need what you have just learnt: Wohin? with nach, zu and in (zur Arbeit, in die Stadt, nach Hause) and the modal verbs können, müssen, wollen, dürfen (Man darf hier nicht parken. Man kann das Rad reparieren lassen). Read for the gist first, then find one place or one number per question.
help.tips[0].text: Wohin? asks for the direction. nach for cities, countries and nach Hause: nach Münster, nach Hause. zu for people, shops and institutions, with dative: zur Arbeit (zu der), zum Bahnhof (zu dem), zum Arzt, zur Uni. in for buildings and places you enter, with accusative: in die Stadt, in den Park, ins Kino (in das). Remember the pair: Wo? in der Stadt (dative) but Wohin? in die Stadt (accusative).
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: In the morning people ride to work, to university or into town.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: In the evening everyone rides home again.
help.tips[0].check.why: zu + der Bahnhof → zum Bahnhof. nach is for cities, in der is Wo?, not Wohin?.
help.tips[1].title: Modal verbs: können, müssen, dürfen, wollen
help.tips[1].text: The modal verb takes position 2, the main verb goes to the end in the infinitive: Man kann das Rad hier parken. Man muss das Rad abschließen. Man darf hier nicht fahren (not allowed). Ich will ein Rad kaufen (want). Forms: ich kann / du kannst / er kann; ich muss / er muss; ich darf / er darf; ich will / er will. man takes the er form.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: In the Radstation you can park the bike and have it repaired.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: On the Promenade cars may not drive. Here they must stay outside.
help.tips[1].check.why: nicht dürfen = not allowed. nicht können = not able, nicht müssen = not necessary.
help.remember[0]: Wohin? nach Hause / nach Münster; zur Arbeit, zum Bahnhof; in die Stadt, ins Kino.
help.remember[1]: Modal verb in position 2, infinitive at the end: Man kann hier parken. Man darf hier nicht fahren.
help.exam: Short texts about a city and getting around, with directions and multiple-choice questions, are a typical reading task at this level.
help.hook: A city with more bicycles than people, a bike garage for 3,300 bikes and a ring road where cars are not allowed. Read how Münster rides.
passageTranslation:
Münster lies in the west of Germany. The city has about three hundred and twenty thousand inhabitants and about five hundred thousand bicycles. That is more bicycles than people! In Münster people do not say Fahrrad, they say Leeze.

Every morning people ride their bikes to work, to university or into town. Almost every second person rides a bike, even in winter and in the rain. The students ride to the university, the children to school, the parents to the supermarket. In the evening everyone rides home.

At the main station stands the Radstation. That is a car park only for bicycles. You can park three thousand three hundred bikes there. You can also have your bike repaired, have it washed or rent a bike.

Around the old town runs the Promenade. That is a green ring, four and a half kilometres long. No cars may drive here, only bicycles and pedestrians. But you must be careful: very many bikes ride very fast here!

Whoever lives in Münster needs no car. But they must have a good lock: every year many bikes are stolen.

questions[0].questionTranslation: About how many bicycles does Münster have?
questions[1].explanation: "In Münster sagt man nicht Fahrrad, man sagt Leeze."
questions[1].optionsTranslation[0]: a long street in Münster on which only bicycles ride
questions[1].optionsTranslation[1]: the word for bicycle in Münster
questions[2].explanation: "Die Studenten fahren zur Universität, die Kinder zur Schule, die Eltern zum Supermarkt."
questions[2].questionTranslation: Where do the children ride in the morning?
questions[3].explanation: nach Hause is a fixed phrase for going home, like nach + city.
questions[3].questionTranslation: 'In the evening everyone rides home.' Why nach and not zu?
questions[3].optionsTranslation[0]: because nach Hause is a fixed phrase, like nach Berlin
questions[3].optionsTranslation[1]: because Haus is a building and buildings always take nach
questions[4].explanation: "Am Hauptbahnhof steht die Radstation. Das ist ein Parkhaus nur für Fahrräder."
questions[4].optionsTranslation[1]: a car park only for bicycles at the main station
questions[4].optionsTranslation[2]: a big shop for cars and bicycles at the main station
questions[5].explanation: The Radstation is only for bikes: park, repair, wash, rent. No cars.
questions[5].questionTranslation: What can you NOT do in the Radstation?
questions[6].explanation: "Hier dürfen keine Autos fahren, nur Fahrräder und Fußgänger."
questions[6].questionTranslation: Who may ride on the Promenade?
questions[6].optionsTranslation[2]: only buses and taxis, but no private cars
questions[7].explanation: "Aber er muss ein gutes Schloss haben: Jedes Jahr werden viele Räder gestohlen."
questions[7].questionTranslation: What must you have in Münster, and why?
questions[7].optionsTranslation[0]: a car, because the city is big
questions[7].optionsTranslation[1]: a good lock, because many bikes are stolen
questions[7].optionsTranslation[2]: an umbrella, because it rains very often and very long in Münster
